questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Three blocks of different masses connected with inextensible string are pulled by a force $F$ on a frictionless surface as shown in the figure. The ratio of tensions $T_1$ to $T_2$ is
questions.solution:
Let the common acceleration of the system be $a$.

Total mass of the system, $M = 2\text{ kg} + 8\text{ kg} + 12\text{ kg} = 22\text{ kg}$.

The acceleration is given by $a = \dfrac{F}{22}$.

The tension $T_1$ is responsible for pulling the blocks of mass $2\text{ kg}$ and $8\text{ kg}$ together.

Equation of motion for this combined mass is:
$T_1 = (2 + 8)a = 10a$

The tension $T_2$ is responsible for pulling only the block of mass $2\text{ kg}$.

Equation of motion for the $2\text{ kg}$ block is:
$T_2 = 2a$

The ratio of the tensions is:
$\dfrac{T_1}{T_2} = \dfrac{10a}{2a} = \dfrac{5}{1}$

Therefore, $T_1 : T_2 = 5 : 1$.

Answer: $5 : 1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The weight of man in lift moving in upward direction with an acceleration 'a' is $660$ N. When the lift moves in the downward direction with the same acceleration, his weight is found to be $380$ N. The real weight of the man when the lift is at rest is
questions.solution:
Let the mass of the man be $m$ and the acceleration of the lift be $a$.

When the lift moves upwards with acceleration $a$, the apparent weight is given by:

$W_1 = m(g + a) = 660$

When the lift moves downwards with acceleration $a$, the apparent weight is given by:

$W_2 = m(g - a) = 380$

Adding the two equations, we get:

$m(g + a) + m(g - a) = 660 + 380$

$2mg = 1040$

$mg = 520$ N

The real weight of the man when the lift is at rest is $mg = 520$ N.

Answer: $520$ N

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A stone of mass $40$ g is tied to a light inextensible string of length $50$ cm and whirled in a vertical circle at the rate of $30$ revolutions per minute. The tension in the string when it is at the lowest point of the circle is
(Take gravitational acceleration, $g = 10\,\text{m/s}^2$ and $\pi^2 = 10$)
questions.solution:
Mass of the stone, $m = 40$ g $= 0.04$ kg

Length of the string, $r = 50$ cm $= 0.5$ m

Frequency of revolution, $f = 30$ rev/min $= \dfrac{30}{60}$ rev/s $= 0.5$ rev/s

Angular velocity, $\omega = 2\pi f = 2\pi \times 0.5 = \pi$ rad/s

At the lowest point of the vertical circle, the net force towards the center provides the necessary centripetal force. The forces acting on the stone are tension $T$ upwards and weight $mg$ downwards.

$T - mg = m\omega^2 r$

$T = m(g + \omega^2 r)$

Substituting the given values and using $\pi^2 = 10$:

$T = 0.04(10 + \pi^2 \times 0.5)$

$T = 0.04(10 + 10 \times 0.5)$

$T = 0.04(10 + 5)$

$T = 0.04 \times 15 = 0.6$ N

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Which of the following person is in an inertial frame of reference?
options: A pilot in an aeroplane which is taking off.
A driver driving a bus which is moving with constant velocity.
A child revolving in a merry - go - round.
A man in a train which is slowing down to stop.
questions.solution:
An inertial frame of reference is a frame that is non-accelerating. It is either at rest or moving with a constant velocity.

An aeroplane taking off has a net forward acceleration, making it a non-inertial frame.

A child revolving in a merry-go-round undergoes circular motion and experiences centripetal acceleration, making it a non-inertial frame.

A train slowing down is decelerating, meaning it has a non-zero acceleration, making it a non-inertial frame.

A bus moving with constant velocity has zero acceleration. Therefore, the driver in the bus is in an inertial frame of reference.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An inextensible string passing over a smooth pulley connects two blocks of masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ ($m_2 \gt  m_1$) vertically. If the acceleration of the system is $\left(\dfrac{g}{n}\right)$, then the ratio of masses $\left(\dfrac{m_2}{m_1}\right)$ is
questions.solution:
For an Atwood machine with masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ ($m_2 \gt m_1$), the acceleration $a$ is given by:

$a = \dfrac{m_2 - m_1}{m_2 + m_1}g$

Given that $a = \dfrac{g}{n}$, we can write:

$\dfrac{m_2 - m_1}{m_2 + m_1}g = \dfrac{g}{n}$

$\dfrac{m_2 - m_1}{m_2 + m_1} = \dfrac{1}{n}$

Dividing the numerator and denominator of the left side by $m_1$:

$\dfrac{\dfrac{m_2}{m_1} - 1}{\dfrac{m_2}{m_1} + 1} = \dfrac{1}{n}$

Cross-multiplying yields:

$n\left(\dfrac{m_2}{m_1} - 1\right) = \dfrac{m_2}{m_1} + 1$

$n\dfrac{m_2}{m_1} - n = \dfrac{m_2}{m_1} + 1$

$\dfrac{m_2}{m_1}(n - 1) = n + 1$

$\dfrac{m_2}{m_1} = \dfrac{n + 1}{n - 1}$

Answer: $\dfrac{n+1}{n-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A block of mass M is lying on a horizontal frictionless surface. One end of the uniform rope of half the mass of the block is fixed to the block which is pulled in the horizontal direction by applying a force F at the other end. The tension in the middle of the rope will be
questions.solution:
Mass of the block = $M$

Mass of the rope = $\dfrac{M}{2}$

Total mass of the system = $M + \dfrac{M}{2} = \dfrac{3M}{2}$

Acceleration of the system $a = \dfrac{F}{\dfrac{3M}{2}} = \dfrac{2F}{3M}$

The tension in the middle of the rope accelerates the block and the rear half of the rope.

Mass behind the middle point $m' = M + \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{M}{2}\right) = M + \dfrac{M}{4} = \dfrac{5M}{4}$

Tension at the middle of the rope $T = m' a = \left(\dfrac{5M}{4}\right)\left(\dfrac{2F}{3M}\right) = \dfrac{5F}{6}$

Answer: $\dfrac{5F}{6}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A car of mass m is crossing the convex bridge of radius of curvature R with speed V. At the highest point the thrust is ($g$ = gravitational acceleration)
questions.solution:
At the highest point of the convex bridge, the forces acting on the car are its weight $mg$ acting downwards and the normal reaction $N$ acting upwards.

The net force towards the center of the circular path provides the necessary centripetal force.

$mg - N = \dfrac{mv^2}{R}$

$N = mg - \dfrac{mv^2}{R}$

The thrust exerted by the car on the bridge is equal in magnitude to the normal reaction $N$.

Answer: $mg - \dfrac{mv^2}{R}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two massless springs of spring constants $K_1$ and $K_2$ are connected one after the other forming a single chain, suspended vertically and a certain mass is attached to the free end. If $x_1$ and $x_2$ are their respective extensions and 'F' is their stretching force, the total extension produced is
questions.solution:
When springs are connected in series, the same stretching force $F$ acts on each spring.

The extension in the first spring is $x_1 = \dfrac{F}{K_1}$

The extension in the second spring is $x_2 = \dfrac{F}{K_2}$

The total extension produced is $x = x_1 + x_2$

$x = \dfrac{F}{K_1} + \dfrac{F}{K_2} = F\left(\dfrac{1}{K_1} + \dfrac{1}{K_2}\right)$

Answer: $F(1/K_1 + 1/K_2)$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A ball is dropped on the floor from a height of 20 m . It rebounds to a height of 5 m . Ball remains in contact with floor for 1 s . The average acceleration during contact is
(acceleration due to gravity $=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2$ )
questions.solution:
A ball dropped from $h_1 = 20\text{m}$ with $g = 10\text{m/s}^2$ reaches the ground with velocity $v_{\text{before}} = -\sqrt{2gh_1} = -\sqrt{2 \times 10 \times 20} = -20\text{m/s}$.

After rebounding to $h_2 = 5\text{m}$, its upward velocity is $v_{\text{after}} = \sqrt{2gh_2} = \sqrt{2 \times 10 \times 5} = 10\text{m/s}$.

During the $\Delta t = 1\text{s}$ contact, the average acceleration is
$a_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \frac{v_{\text{after}} - v_{\text{before}}}{\Delta t} = \frac{10 - (-20)}{1} = 30\text{m/s}^2$.

The average acceleration is $\boxed{\text{A}}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In the arrangement shown in the figure, the mass ' m ' will ascend with an acceleration (consider pully and rope are massless) ( $g=$ acceleration due to gravity)
questions.solution:
For mass m accelerating upward against gravity, the net force yields $T - mg = ma$.

The heavier mass $\frac{3}{2}m$ descends with $\frac{3}{2}mg - T = \frac{3}{2}ma$.

Adding equations eliminates tension: $(T - mg) + (\frac{3}{2}mg - T) = ma + \frac{3}{2}ma \Rightarrow \frac{1}{2}mg = \frac{5}{2}ma$.

Solving for acceleration gives $a = \frac{\frac{1}{2}g}{\frac{5}{2}} = \frac{g}{5}$.

The acceleration of mass m is $\frac{g}{5}$ upward.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A mass ' $M$ ' is suspended by a rope from a rigid support at point ' $P$ ' as shown in figure. Another rope is tied at end 'Q' and pulled horizontally with a force ' $F$ '. If the rope makes an angle ' $\theta$ ' with vertical then the tension in the string ' PQ ' is
questions.solution:
Tension in the string PQ is determined by analyzing the equilibrium conditions at point Q where the ropes meet. The horizontal tension component balances the applied force $F$, while the vertical component supports the weight $Mg$.

Resolving the tension $T$ into components:
Vertical component: $T\cos\theta$
Horizontal component: $T\sin\theta$

From horizontal equilibrium:
$T\sin\theta = F$

Solving for tension:
$T = \frac{F}{\sin\theta}$

This corresponds to option B.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A machine gun fires a bullet of mass 35 gram with a speed of $600 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$. The person holding the gum can extract a maximum force of 147 N on it. The number of bullets that can be fired from the gun per second is
questions.solution:
The force exerted by the gun equals the rate of change of momentum of the bullets. For each bullet of mass $m = 0.035 \text{ kg}$ fired at speed $v = 600 \text{ m/s}$, the momentum per bullet is $mv$.

If $n$ bullets are fired per second, the rate of change of momentum is $n \cdot (m v)$.

Using Newton’s second law, $F = n m v$, with $F = 147 \text{ N}$:

$147 = n \cdot (0.035 \times 600)$

Since $0.035 \times 600 = 21$, we have:

$147 = 21n$

Solving for $n$:

$n = \frac{147}{21} = 7$

Final answer: $\boxed{7}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle describes a horizontal circle on smooth inner surface of a cone as shown in figure. If the height of the circle above the vertex is 10 cm . The speed of the particle is (g, acceleration due to gravity $=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2$ )
questions.solution:
A particle moves in uniform circular motion on the smooth inner surface of a cone. The vertical component of the normal force balances gravity, while the horizontal component provides centripetal force.

Resolving the normal force $N$ acting perpendicular to the surface: $N \cos\theta = mg$ vertically, and $N \sin\theta = mv^2/R$ horizontally. Eliminating $N$ gives $\tan\theta = v^2/(Rg)$.

From the cone's geometry, $\tan\theta = h/R$. Substituting yields:

$v^2 = Rg \cdot \frac{h}{R} = gh$

With $h = 0.1 \text{ m}$ and $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$, we obtain:

$v^2 = (10)(0.1) = 1 \text{ m}^2/\text{s}^2$
$v = 1 \text{ m/s}$

Final answer: $\boxed{\text{C}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A motor cyclist has to rotate in horizontal circles inside the cylindrical wall of inner radius ' R ' metre. If the coefficient of friction between the wall and the tyres is ' $\mu_{\mathrm{s}}$ ', then the minimum speed required is ( $\mathrm{g}=$ acceleration due to gravity)
questions.solution:
The minimum speed required for a motorcyclist to ride on a vertical cylindrical wall is derived from equilibrium conditions. The normal force provides centripetal acceleration: $N = \frac{mv^2}{R}$.

Vertical equilibrium requires that friction balances weight: $\mu_s N \ge mg$. At minimum speed, equality holds: $\mu_s N = mg$.

Substituting the expression for normal force yields $\mu_s \left(\frac{mv^2}{R}\right) = mg$. Mass cancels, giving $\mu_s \frac{v^2}{R} = g$.

Solving for velocity: $v^2 = \frac{Rg}{\mu_s}$, so $v = \sqrt{\frac{Rg}{\mu_s}}$.

The final answer is $\sqrt{\frac{Rg}{\mu_s}}$, corresponding to option B.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The figure shows two masses ' m ' and ' M ' connected by a light string that passes through a small hole 'O' at the centre of the table. Mass ' m ' is moved round in a horizontal circle with 'O' as the centre. The frequency with which ' m ' should be revolved so that ' M ' remains stationary is (g = gravitational acceleration)
questions.solution:
Equilibrium requires that the tension force matches the weight of mass $M$: $T = Mg$.

The centripetal force for mass $m$ revolving with angular frequency $\omega$ at radius $L$ is provided by tension: $T = m \omega^2 L$.

Equating gives $Mg = m \omega^2 L$.

Substituting $\omega = 2\pi f$ yields $Mg = m (2\pi f)^2 L = 4\pi^2 m f^2 L$.

Solving for frequency: $f = \frac{1}{2\pi} \sqrt{\frac{Mg}{mL}}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The weight of man in a stationary lift is $\mathrm{w}_1$ and when it is moving downwards with uniform acceleration ' $a$ ' is $w_2$. If the ratio $\mathrm{w}_1: \mathrm{w}_2=4: 3$, then the value of ' a ' is ( $\mathrm{g}=$ acceleration due to gravity)
questions.solution:
Let m represent the man's mass and g the acceleration due to gravity. When stationary, the apparent weight equals the actual weight: $w_1 = mg$.

With downward acceleration a, the apparent weight becomes $w_2 = m(g - a)$.

Given $w_1 : w_2 = 4 : 3$, so $\frac{w_1}{w_2} = \frac{4}{3}$. Substituting, $\frac{mg}{m(g - a)} = \frac{4}{3}$.

Simplification yields $\frac{g}{g - a} = \frac{4}{3}$, and cross-multiplying gives $3g = 4(g - a)$.

Solving this, $3g = 4g - 4a$, so $4a = g$, hence $a = \frac{g}{4}$.

Option B is correct.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Radius of curved road is ' R ', width of road is ' b '. The outer edge of road is raised by ' $h$ ' with respect to inner edge so that a car with velocity ' $V$ ' can pass safe over it, then value of ' $h$ ' is ( $g=$ acceleration due to gravity)
questions.solution:
For a car moving with velocity $V$ on a banked road of radius $R$, the horizontal component of the normal force provides the centripripetal force, while the vertical component balances gravity. For a banking angle $\theta$:

$N \sin\theta = \frac{mV^2}{R}$
$N \cos\theta = mg$

Dividing these expressions yields $\tan\theta = \frac{V^2}{Rg}$.

From the road geometry with width $b$ and outer edge raised by $h$, $\tan\theta = \frac{h}{b}$. Equating gives:

$\frac{h}{b} = \frac{V^2}{Rg}$

Solving for the height difference: $h = \frac{V^2 b}{Rg}$, which corresponds to option A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two bodies of mass 10 kg and 5 kg are moving in concentric circular orbits of radii ' R ' and ' r ' respectively such that their periods are same. The ratio between their centripetal acceleration is
questions.solution:
The centripetal acceleration $a$ for a body in uniform circular motion with orbital radius $R$ and period $T$ is given by $a = \frac{4\pi^2 R}{T^2}$.

Since both bodies have the same period $T$, the ratio of accelerations $\frac{a_1}{a_2} = \frac{R_1}{R_2} = \frac{R}{r}$.

Final Answer: $\boxed{\text{A}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A car is driven on the banked road of radius of curvature 20 m with maximum safe speed. In order to increase its safety speed by $20 \%$, without changing the angle of banking, the increase in the radius of curvature will be
[Assume friction is same on the road]
questions.solution:
The maximum safe speed on a banked road with friction is given by $v = \sqrt{rg \frac{\tan\theta + \mu}{1 - \mu \tan\theta}}$, where $\theta$ and $\mu$ remain constant. Denoting the constant term as $K$, this simplifies to $v = \sqrt{rgK}$.

Squaring both sides yields $v^2 = rgK$, showing $v^2$ is directly proportional to $r$.

Given $v_2 = 1.2v_1$ and $r_1 = 20\text{ m}$, the proportionality gives $\frac{v_2^2}{v_1^2} = \frac{r_2}{r_1}$. Substituting $v_2 = 1.2v_1$ produces $1.44 = \frac{r_2}{20}$.

Solving, $r_2 = 28.8\text{ m}$ and the increase is $\Delta r = 8.8\text{ m}$.

$\boxed{8.8\text{ m}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A constant force acts on two different masses independently and produces accelerations $A_1$ and $A_2$. When the same force acts on their combined mass, the acceleration produced is
questions.solution:
A constant force $F$ produces accelerations $A_1$ and $A_2$ on masses $m_1$ and $m_2$, respectively. From Newton's second law:

$F = m_1 A_1 \quad \Rightarrow \quad m_1 = \frac{F}{A_1}$

$F = m_2 A_2 \quad \Rightarrow \quad m_2 = \frac{F}{A_2}$

When the force acts on the combined mass $m_1 + m_2$, the acceleration $A$ satisfies:

$F = (m_1 + m_2)A$

Substituting both mass expressions yields:

$F = \left( \frac{F}{A_1} + \frac{F}{A_2} \right)A = F \left( \frac{1}{A_1} + \frac{1}{A_2} \right)A$

Dividing both sides by $F$ (nonzero):

$1 = \left( \frac{A_1 + A_2}{A_1 A_2} \right)A$

Solving for $A$ gives the final result:

$A = \frac{A_1 A_2}{A_1 + A_2}$

The correct choice is C.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A vehicle is moving with uniform speed along 3 different shaped roads as horizontal, concave and convex. The surface of road on which, the normal reaction on vehicle is maximum is
questions.solution:
The normal reaction on the vehicle is determined by analyzing the forces when moving at uniform speed v on different surfaces.

On a horizontal road, the gravitational force mg is balanced by the normal reaction NH, giving NH = mg.

At the lowest point on a concave road, the centripetal force mv2/r is provided by the normal reaction exceeding gravity: NC − mg = mv2/r, leading to NC = mg + mv2/r.

At the highest point on a convex road, gravity exceeds the normal reaction to provide the centripetal force: mg − NX = mv2/r, so NX = mg − mv2/r.

Comparing the expressions shows NC > NH > NX, indicating the maximum normal reaction occurs on the concave road.

The answer is $\boxed{B}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body of mass 100 gram is tied to a spring of spring constant $8 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}$, while the other end of a spring is fixed. If the body moves in a circular path on smooth horizontal surface with constant angular speed $8 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}$ then the ratio of extension in the spring to its natured length will be
questions.solution:
The centripetal force required for circular motion is provided by the spring force. For a mass $m$ moving with angular speed $\omega$ along a circular path of radius $r = L_0 + x$, where $L_0$ is the natural length and $x$ the extension, the forces balance as $kx = m \omega^2 (L_0 + x)$.

Rearranging gives $x(k - m \omega^2) = m \omega^2 L_0$, so

$\frac{x}{L_0} = \frac{m \omega^2}{k - m \omega^2}$.

With $m = 0.1 \text{ kg}$, $k = 8 \text{ N/m}$, and $\omega = 8 \text{ rad/s}$, we compute $m \omega^2 = 6.4 \text{ N/m}$ and $k - m \omega^2 = 1.6 \text{ N/m}$. The ratio is then $\frac{6.4}{1.6} = 4$.

The extension is four times the natural length.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A conveyor belt is moving with constant velocity (V). Sand is being dropped on the belt at the rate of $\mathrm{M} \mathrm{~kg} / \mathrm{s}$. The force necessary to keep the belt moving with a constant velocity $\mathrm{V} \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}$ will be
questions.solution:
The sand is deposited with zero initial horizontal velocity onto the belt moving at constant velocity $V$. The force needed to maintain constant belt velocity arises solely from accelerating each infinitesimal mass $dm$ to speed $V$.

The rate of mass deposition is $M = \frac{dm}{dt}$, and the change in momentum for mass $dm$ is $dP = (dm) V$.

By Newton's second law, the required force equals the rate of momentum transfer: $F = \frac{dP}{dt} = V \frac{dm}{dt}$.

Substituting the mass flow rate gives $F = M V$.

The force necessary to maintain constant belt velocity is $MV$ N, corresponding to option D.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A child stands on a weighing machine inside a lift. When the lift is going down with acceleration $\frac{g}{3}$, the machine shows a reading 20 N. When the lift goes upwards with acceleration $\frac{g}{3}$, the reading would be ( $\mathrm{g}=$ gravitational acceleration)
questions.solution:
Mass and apparent weight
Let the mass of the child be $m$, and $R$ be the reading on the scale, which equals the normal force exerted on the child.

The apparent weight changes when the elevator accelerates. Applying Newton's second law, $\Sigma F = ma$:

Elevator descending with acceleration $a = \frac{g}{3}$
The forces are the gravitational force $mg$ downward and the normal force $R_1$ upward. Since the acceleration is downward, $mg - R_1 = ma$. Given $R_1 = 20\text{ N}$ and $a = \frac{g}{3}$, we have:

$mg - 20 = \frac{mg}{3}$
$\frac{2mg}{3} = 20$
$mg = 30\text{ N}$

The actual weight is $30\text{ N}$.

Elevator ascending with acceleration $a = \frac{g}{3}$
Now, the net force is upward: $R_2 - mg = ma$. With $mg = 30\text{ N}$ and $a = \frac{g}{3}$, substitute:

$R_2 = 30 + \frac{mg}{3} = 30 + 10 = 40\text{ N}$

The scale reads $\boxed{40\text{ N}}$ when the elevator ascends with acceleration $\frac{g}{3}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A force acting on a body of mass 5 Kg is $(4 \hat{\mathrm{i}}-2 \hat{\mathrm{j}}+3 \hat{\mathrm{k}}) \mathrm{N}$. If the body is initially at rest then the magnitude of its velocity at the end of 10 second in $\mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}$ will be
questions.solution:
Newton's second law gives the acceleration as $\mathrm{a} = \frac{\mathrm{F}}{m} = \frac{4\hat{\mathrm{i}} - 2\hat{\mathrm{j}} + 3\hat{\mathrm{k}}}{5} = (0.8\hat{\mathrm{i}} - 0.4\hat{\mathrm{j}} + 0.6\hat{\mathrm{k}})$ m/s2.

Starting from rest, the velocity after 10 s is $\mathrm{v} = \mathrm{a}t = (0.8\hat{\mathrm{i}} - 0.4\hat{\mathrm{j}} + 0.6\hat{\mathrm{k}}) \times 10 = (8\hat{\mathrm{i}} - 4\hat{\mathrm{j}} + 6\hat{\mathrm{k}})$ m/s.

The magnitude is $|\mathrm{v}| = \sqrt{8^2 + (-4)^2 + 6^2} = \sqrt{64 + 16 + 36} = \sqrt{116} = 2\sqrt{29}$ m/s.

Answer: $\mathrm{B}$

questions.q: Which one of the following person is in an inertial frame of reference?
options: A person (man) in a train which is slowing down to stop.
A person (child) revolving in a merry-go-round.
A person (driver) in a bus which is moving with constant velocity.
A person (pilot) in an aeroplane which is taking off.
questions.solution:
An inertial frame of reference is defined as one moving with constant velocity (including rest), where Newton's first law holds true. Frames undergoing acceleration are non-inertial.

A person on a train slowing down experiences deceleration, indicating a non-inertial frame.

Circular motion on a merry-go-round involves centripetal acceleration, also non-inertial.

A bus moving at constant velocity has zero acceleration, making it an inertial frame.

An airplane taking off accelerates during departure, resulting in a non-inertial frame.

Only the bus driver moving at constant velocity occupies an inertial frame:

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A solid sphere rolls without slipping on an inclined plane at an angle $\theta$. The ratio of total kinetic energy to its rotational kinetic energy is
questions.solution:
Moment of Inertia of a solid sphere, $I=\frac{2}{5} \mathrm{MR}^2$
Since there is no slipping,
$\mathrm{v}=\mathrm{R} \omega\therefore \quad$ Rotational kinetic energy $\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{Tot}}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{I} \omega^2\begin{aligned}
& =\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{2}{5} \times \mathrm{M} \times \mathrm{R}^2 \times \omega^2 \\
& =\frac{\mathrm{MR}^2 \omega^2}{5} \\
& =\frac{\mathrm{MV}^2}{5}... (i)
\end{aligned}$
Total kinetic energy
$\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{K}} & =\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{I}^2+\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{MV}^2 \\
& =\frac{\mathrm{MV}^2}{5}+\frac{\mathrm{MV}^2}{2} \\
& =\frac{7 \mathrm{MV}^2}{10}... (ii)
\end{aligned}$
Dividing (ii) by (i), we get,
$\frac{\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{K}}}{\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{me}}}=\frac{\left(\frac{7 \mathrm{MV}^2}{10}\right)}{\left(\frac{\mathrm{MV}^2}{5}\right)}=\frac{7}{2}$

questions.q: Two massless springs of spring constant $K_1$ and $K_2$ are connected one after the other forming a single chain, suspended vertically and certain mass is attached to the free end. If $e_1$ and $e_2$ are their respective extensions and $f$ is their stretching force, the total extension produced is
questions.solution:
The total restoring force is related to extension as follows:
$f=-K x \quad---(1)$
The extension in the springs are related to the restoring force as follows:
$f=-K_1 e_1---(2)$
and
$f=-K_2 e_2---(3)$
The total extension of the springs is:
$x=e_1+e_2---(4)$
Using equation (1),(2) and (3)
$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow\left(-\frac{f}{K}\right)=\left(-\frac{f}{K_1}\right)+\left(-\frac{f}{K_2}\right) \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{1}{K}=\left(\frac{1}{K_1}+\frac{1}{K_2}\right)---(5)\end{aligned}$
The total extension using equation (4) and (5)is given by,
$x=\frac{f}{K}=f\left(\frac{1}{K_1}+\frac{1}{K_2}\right)$

[Angle of banking and friction is unchanged in both the cases.]
questions.solution:
For road safety on a banked road, the velocity of the car has following scaling relation with respect to the curvature:
$v^2 \propto R$
So,
$v^2=C R---(1)$
where $C$ is a constant that involves the banking angle and friction.
If the new velocity is $v^{\prime}=1.1 v$ as $10 \%$ higher speed, then
$v^{\prime 2}=C R^{\prime}---(2)$
where, $R^{\prime}$ is the new radius of curvature due to safely.
Now, take the ratio of equation (1) and (2)
$\begin{aligned}
& \left(\frac{v^{\prime}}{v}\right)^2=\frac{R^{\prime}}{R} \\
& \Rightarrow(1.1)^2=\frac{R^{\prime}}{R} \\
& \Rightarrow \frac{(1.1)^2-1}{1}=\frac{R^{\prime}-R}{R}
\end{aligned}\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \frac{0.21}{1}=\frac{\left(R^{\prime}-R\right)}{R} \\ & \Rightarrow\left(R^{\prime}-R\right)=0.21 R=0.21 \times 20 \mathrm{~m}=4.2 \mathrm{~m}\end{aligned}$

(Acceleration due to gravity, $g=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2$ )
questions.solution:
The correct option is (B).
Concept: For safe driving, the centripetal force must be less than limiting friction otherwise the vehicle will skid away from the road.
Mathematically it can be written as
$\frac{\mathrm{mv}}{\mathrm{r}} \leq \mu \mathrm{mg}$
where $m$ is the mass, $v$ is the velocity, $\mu$ is the coefficient of friction and $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity.
On plugging the values given in the question,
$r_{\min }=\frac{v^2}{\mu g}=\frac{30^2}{0.5 \times 10}=180 \mathrm{~m}$
